cards.summary: Converts an object to array.
cards.description: This is equivalent to `array(a, dtype, copy=False, order=order)`.

params.name: a
params.description: The source object.

params.name: dtype
params.description: Data type specifier. It is inferred from the input by default.

params.name: order
params.description: ({'C', 'F', 'A', 'K'}) Whether to use row-major (C-style) or column-major (Fortran-style) memory representation. Defaults to `'K'`. `order` is ignored for objects that are not `cupy.ndarray`, but have the `__cuda_array_interface__` attribute.

params.name: copy
params.description: (bool, optional) If `True`, `obj` is always copied. If `False`, prohibits copy and raises `ValueError` on failure. If `None` (default), `obj` is copied only when necessary.

params.name: blocking
params.description: (bool) Default is `False`, meaning if a H2D copy is needed it would run asynchronously on the current stream, and users are responsible for ensuring the stream order. For example, writing to the source `a` without proper ordering while copying would result in a race condition. If set to `True`, the copy is synchronous (with respect to the host).

cards.returns: cupy.ndarray: An array on the current device. If `a` is already on the device, no copy is performed.
cards.notes:
If `a` is an `numpy.ndarray` instance that contains big-endian data,
this function automatically swaps its byte order to little-endian,
which is the NVIDIA and AMD GPU architecture's native use.
pitfalls: Copies host data to the current GPU. Transfers are often slower than the computation itself, so move data once and keep it on the GPU.
There is no implicit conversion back: `numpy.asarray(cupy_array)` raises `TypeError`. Use `cupy.asnumpy(x)` or `x.get()`.
Python floats and NumPy's default dtype give float64. Pass `dtype=cupy.float32` when single precision is enough: many GPUs (e.g. T4, consumer cards) have far lower FP64 throughput.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp

x_host = np.arange(6, dtype=np.float32).reshape(2, 3)
x = cp.asarray(x_host)             # host -> device copy
y = (x * 2).sum(axis=1)            # computed on the GPU
y_host = cp.asnumpy(y)             # device -> host copy (waits for the GPU)
assert isinstance(y, cp.ndarray) and isinstance(y_host, np.ndarray)
assert np.allclose(y_host, (x_host * 2).sum(axis=1))

params.name: a
params.description: Arbitrary object that can be converted to `numpy.ndarray`.

params.name: stream
params.description: (cupy.cuda.Stream) CUDA stream object. If given, the stream is used to perform the copy. Otherwise, the current stream is used. Note that if `a` is not a `cupy.ndarray` object, then this argument has no effect.

params.name: order
params.description: ({'C', 'F', 'A'}) The desired memory layout of the host array. When `order` is 'A', it uses 'F' if the array is fortran-contiguous and 'C' otherwise. The `order` will be ignored if `out` is specified.

params.name: out
params.description: (numpy.ndarray) The output array to be written to. It must have compatible shape and dtype with those of `a`'s.

params.description: (bool) If set to `False`, the copy runs asynchronously on the given (if given) or current stream, and users are responsible for ensuring the stream order. Default is `True`, so the copy is synchronous (with respect to the host).

pitfalls: Blocks until the GPU work that produces the array has finished (`blocking=True` by default). It is the usual implicit synchronization point; GPU timings taken without a sync measure only kernel launches.
`x.get()` does the same for a `cupy.ndarray`.

import numpy as np
import cupy as cp

x = cp.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5, dtype=cp.float32)
host = cp.asnumpy(x)               # same as x.get()
assert isinstance(host, np.ndarray)
assert np.allclose(host, np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5))

cards.summary: Solves multiple linear matrix equations using cublas<t>getr[fs]Batched().
cards.description: Computes the solution to system of linear equation `ax = b`.

params.name: a
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) The matrix with dimension `(..., M, M)`.

params.name: b
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) The matrix with dimension `(..., M)` or `(..., M, K)`.

cards.returns: cupy.ndarray: The matrix with dimension `(..., M)` or `(..., M, K)`.
pitfalls: `import cupy` does not load `cupy.cublas`: use `from cupy import cublas` or `import cupy.cublas`, otherwise `cupy.cublas.batched_gesv` raises `AttributeError`.
Unlike `cupy.linalg.solve`, it accepts one right-hand-side vector per system, shape `(..., M)`, as well as `(..., M, K)`.
`cupy.linalg.solve` already calls it for stacked matrices up to `cupy.cublas.get_batched_gesv_limit()`; above that size batched LU is slow, so prefer `cupy.linalg.solve` for large matrices.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
from cupy import cublas                           # `import cupy` alone does not load it

A = cp.random.rand(64, 12, 12) + 12 * cp.eye(12)
y = cp.random.rand(64, 12)                        # one right-hand side per system
x = cublas.batched_gesv(A, y)                     # stacked vectors are accepted here
assert x.shape == (64, 12)
assert np.allclose(cp.einsum('bij,bj->bi', A, x).get(), y.get())

cards.signature: gemm(transa, transb, a, b, out=None, alpha=1.0, beta=0.0)
cards.summary: Computes out = alpha * op(a) @ op(b) + beta * out
cards.description:
op(a) = a if transa is 'N', op(a) = a.T if transa is 'T',
op(a) = a.T.conj() if transa is 'H'.
op(b) = b if transb is 'N', op(b) = b.T if transb is 'T',
op(b) = b.T.conj() if transb is 'H'.
pitfalls: `import cupy` does not load `cupy.cublas`: `cupy.cublas.gemm(...)` after only `import cupy` raises `AttributeError`. Use `from cupy import cublas` (as in the example) or `import cupy.cublas`.
`transa`/`transb` take 'N', 'T' or 'H' and apply op() to the inputs without materializing a transposed copy.
Only 2-D operands. Use `cupy.matmul` for batched products.
With `out` given, the result is accumulated in place: `out = alpha * op(a) @ op(b) + beta * out`.

import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
from cupy import cublas

a = cp.random.rand(64, 32)
b = cp.random.rand(64, 16)
c = cublas.gemm('T', 'N', a, b)                   # a.T @ b without a transposed copy
assert np.allclose(c.get(), a.get().T @ b.get())

cards.description:
For arrays with more than one axis, it computes the dot product along the
last axis of `a` and the second-to-last axis of `b`. This is just a
matrix product if the both arrays are 2-D. For 1-D arrays, it uses their
unique axis as an axis to take dot product over.

params.name: a

params.name: b

params.name: out

cards.summary: Evaluates the Einstein summation convention on the operands.
cards.description:
Using the Einstein summation convention, many common multi-dimensional array operations can be represented in a simple fashion. This function provides a way to compute such summations.

.. _cuQuantum Python: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuquantum/python/

params.name: operands
params.description: (sequence of arrays) These are the arrays for the operation.

cards.returns: cupy.ndarray: The calculation based on the Einstein summation convention.
cards.notes:
- Memory contiguity of the returned array is not always compatible with
  that of `numpy.einsum`.
- `out`, `order`, and `casting` options are not supported.
- If `CUPY_ACCELERATORS` includes `cutensornet`, the `einsum`
  calculation will be performed by the cuTensorNet backend if possible.

    - The support of the `optimize` option is limited (currently, only
      `False`, 'cutensornet', or a custom path for pairwise contraction
      is supported, and the maximum intermediate size is ignored). If
      you need finer control for path optimization, consider replacing
      `cupy.einsum` by `cuquantum.contract` instead.
    - Requires `cuQuantum Python` (v22.03+).

- If `CUPY_ACCELERATORS` includes `cutensor`, `einsum` will be
  accelerated by the cuTENSOR backend whenever possible.
pitfalls: Pairwise contractions are reduced to `tensordot`/cuBLAS GEMMs by default. With `CUPY_ACCELERATORS=cutensor` and cuTENSOR installed, CuPy can use cuTENSOR contractions instead.
Expressions like `'bij,bj->bi'` (batched matrix-vector) are a clear, fast alternative to `matmul` with reshaping.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp

A = cp.random.rand(32, 8, 8)
x = cp.random.rand(32, 8)
y = cp.einsum('bij,bj->bi', A, x)                 # batched matrix-vector product
assert np.allclose(y.get(), np.einsum('bij,bj->bi', A.get(), x.get()))

params.name: a
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) Array to be transform.

params.name: n
params.description: (None or int) Length of the transformed axis of the output. If `n` is not given, the length of the input along the axis specified by `axis` is used.

params.name: axis
params.description: (int) Axis over which to compute the FFT.

params.description: (`"backward"`, `"ortho"`, or `"forward"`) Optional keyword to specify the normalization mode. Default is `None`, which is an alias of `"backward"`.

cards.returns: cupy.ndarray: The transformed array which shape is specified by `n` and type will convert to complex if the input is other.
pitfalls: Single precision is preserved: float16/float32/complex64 input gives complex64 output; other real or integer input gives complex128. NumPy < 2 always returned complex128.
cuFFT plans are cached per device (`cupy.fft.config.get_plan_cache()`). The first call for a new shape/dtype pays the planning cost, so warm up before timing.
Lengths with only small prime factors (2, 3, 5, 7) are fastest; `cupyx.scipy.fft.next_fast_len(n)` gives a good padded length.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp

x = cp.random.rand(1024, dtype=cp.float32)
X = cp.fft.fft(x)
assert X.dtype == cp.complex64                    # precision is kept
assert np.allclose(X.get(), np.fft.fft(x.get()), rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-3)

cards.summary: Return the least-squares solution to a linear matrix equation.
cards.description:
Solves the equation `a x = b` by computing a vector `x` that
minimizes the Euclidean 2-norm `|| b - a x ||^2`.  The equation may
be under-, well-, or over- determined (i.e., the number of
linearly independent rows of `a` can be less than, equal to, or
greater than its number of linearly independent columns).  If `a`
is square and of full rank, then `x` (but for round-off error) is
the "exact" solution of the equation.

params.name: a
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) "Coefficient" matrix with dimension `(M, N)`

params.name: b
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) "Dependent variable" values with dimension `(M,)` or `(M, K)`

params.name: rcond
params.description: (float, optional) Cutoff parameter for small singular values. For stability it computes the largest singular value denoted by `s`, and sets all singular values smaller than `s` to zero.

cards.returns: tuple: A tuple of `(x, residuals, rank, s)`. Note `x` is the least-squares solution with shape `(N,)` or `(N, K)` depending if `b` was two-dimensional. The sums of `residuals` is the squared Euclidean 2-norm for each column in b - a*x. The `residuals` is an empty array if the rank of a is < N or M <= N, but iff b is 1-dimensional, this is a (1,) shape array, Otherwise the shape is (K,). The `rank` of matrix `a` is an integer. The singular values of `a` are `s`.
cards.warnings: This function calls one or more cuSOLVER routine(s) which may yield invalid results if input conditions are not met. To detect these invalid results, you can set the `linalg` configuration to a value that is not `ignore` in `cupyx.errstate` or `cupyx.seterr`.
pitfalls: Implemented with an SVD (`full_matrices=False`): robust for rank-deficient problems, but slower than QR. For tall, well-conditioned problems `qr` + `cupyx.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular` is faster.
Returns a 4-tuple `(x, residuals, rank, s)`. `rcond=None` uses `eps * max(M, N)` (the NumPy 2 default).
Only 2-D `a` is supported; there is no batched least squares.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp

m, n = 500, 20
A = cp.random.rand(m, n)
x_true = cp.arange(n, dtype=A.dtype)
b = A @ x_true
x, residuals, rank, s = cp.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
assert int(rank) == n
assert np.allclose(x.get(), x_true.get(), atol=1e-6)

x = cp.linalg.solve(a, b)
assert np.allclose((a @ x).get(), b.get())

# 32 independent 8x8 systems, each with its own right-hand side vector
A = cp.random.rand(32, 8, 8) + 8 * cp.eye(8)
B = cp.random.rand(32, 8)
X = cp.linalg.solve(A, B[..., None])[..., 0]      # b must be (..., M, K)
assert np.allclose(cp.einsum('bij,bj->bi', A, X).get(), B.get())

Mixed dtypes promote like NumPy (float32 @ float64 -> float64), which can be much slower on GPUs with low FP64 throughput.

import numpy as np
import cupy as cp

a = cp.random.rand(8, 64, 32, dtype=cp.float32)   # batch of 8 matrices
b = cp.random.rand(8, 32, 16, dtype=cp.float32)
c = cp.matmul(a, b)                               # one batched GEMM; same as a @ b
assert c.shape == (8, 64, 16) and c.dtype == cp.float32
assert np.allclose(c.get(), a.get() @ b.get(), rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)

cards.signature: dct(x, type=2, n=None, axis=-1, norm=None, overwrite_x=False)
cards.summary: Return the Discrete Cosine Transform of an array, x.

params.name: x
params.description: cupy.ndarray The input array.

params.name: type
params.description: {1, 2, 3, 4}, optional Type of the DCT (see Notes). Default type is 2. Currently CuPy only supports types 2 and 3.

params.name: n
params.description: int, optional: Length of the transform. If `n < x.shape[axis]`, `x` is truncated. If `n > x.shape[axis]`, `x` is zero-padded. The default results in `n = x.shape[axis]`.

params.name: axis
params.description: int, optional Axis along which the dct is computed; the default is over the last axis (i.e., `axis=-1`).

params.name: norm
params.description: {"backward", "ortho", "forward"}, optional Normalization mode (see Notes). Default is "backward".

params.name: overwrite_x
params.description: bool, optional If True, the contents of `x` can be destroyed; the default is False.

cards.returns: y : cupy.ndarray of real The transformed input array.
cards.notes:
For a single dimension array `x`, `dct(x, norm='ortho')` is equal
to MATLAB `dct(x)`.

For `norm="ortho"` both the `dct` and `idct` are scaled by the same
overall factor in both directions. By default, the transform is also
orthogonalized which for types 1, 2 and 3 means the transform definition is
modified to give orthogonality of the DCT matrix (see below).

For `norm="backward"`, there is no scaling on `dct` and the `idct` is
scaled by `1/N` where `N` is the "logical" size of the DCT. For
`norm="forward"` the `1/N` normalization is applied to the forward
`dct` instead and the `idct` is unnormalized.

refers to DCT type 2, and 'the' Inverse DCT generally refers to DCT
type 3 [1]_. See the `scipy.fft.dct` documentation for a full
description of each type.

cards.summary: Generate a CUDA FFT plan for transforming up to three axes.

params.name: a
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) Array to be transform, assumed to be either C- or F- contiguous.

params.name: shape
params.description: (None or tuple of ints) Shape of the transformed axes of the output. If `shape` is not given, the lengths of the input along the axes specified by `axes` are used.

params.name: axes
params.description: (None or int or tuple of int) The axes of the array to transform. If `None`, it is assumed that all axes are transformed. Currently, for performing N-D transform these must be a set of up to three adjacent axes, and must include either the first or the last axis of the array.

params.description: (str) The FFT type to perform. Acceptable values are: * 'C2C': complex-to-complex transform (default) * 'R2C': real-to-complex transform * 'C2R': complex-to-real transform

The returned plan can not only be passed as one of the arguments of
the functions in `cupyx.scipy.fftpack`, but also be used as a
context manager for both `cupy.fft` and `cupyx.scipy.fftpack`
functions:


    x = cupy.random.random(16).reshape(4, 4).astype(complex)
    plan = cupyx.scipy.fftpack.get_fft_plan(x)
    with plan:
        y = cupy.fft.fftn(x)
        # alternatively:
        y = cupyx.scipy.fftpack.fftn(x)  # no explicit plan is given!
    # alternatively:
    y = cupyx.scipy.fftpack.fftn(x, plan=plan)  # pass plan explicitly

If this function is called under the context of
`cupy.fft.config.set_cufft_callbacks`, the generated plan will
have callbacks enabled.
cards.warnings: This API is a deviation from SciPy's, is currently experimental, and may be changed in the future version.
pitfalls: The plan can be used as a context manager (`with plan: y = cupy.fft.fft(x)`) or passed as `plan=` to `cupyx.scipy.fft` functions. Reusing it avoids plan look-ups in hot loops.
`value_type` must match the transform: 'C2C' (default), 'R2C' for rfft, 'C2R' for irfft. A plan whose dtype, size or batch does not match the call raises `ValueError`.
The plan is tied to the array's shape, dtype, layout and the transformed axes.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
import cupyx.scipy.fft as cufft

x = cp.random.rand(64, 128).astype(cp.complex64)
plan = cufft.get_fft_plan(x, axes=(-1,))         # plan a 1-D C2C FFT along the last axis
y = cufft.fft(x, axis=-1, plan=plan)
with plan:                                        # plan also works as a context manager
    y2 = cp.fft.fft(x, axis=-1)
assert np.allclose(y.get(), y2.get())
assert np.allclose(y.get(), np.fft.fft(x.get(), axis=-1), rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-3)

cards.summary: Find the next fast size to `fft`.
cards.description:
.. _cuFFT documentation:
    https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cufft/index.html#accuracy-and-performance

params.description: (int) The size of input array.

cards.notes:
It may return a different value to `scipy.fft.next_fast_len`
as pocketfft's prime factors are different from cuFFT's factors.
For details, see the `cuFFT documentation`.
pitfalls: Pad signals to `next_fast_len(n)` (sizes with small prime factors) before FFT-based convolution or correlation; awkward prime sizes are much slower.
cards.example:

n = next_fast_len(1009)                           # 1009 is prime
assert n >= 1009
x = cp.random.rand(1009)
X = cp.fft.rfft(x, n=n)                           # zero-padded transform
assert X.shape == (n // 2 + 1,)

cards.summary: LU decomposition.
cards.description:
Decomposes a given two-dimensional matrix into `P @ L @ U`, where `P`
is a permutation matrix, `L` is a lower triangular or trapezoidal matrix
with unit diagonal, and `U` is a upper triangular or trapezoidal matrix.

params.name: a
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) The input matrix with dimension `(M, N)`.

params.name: permute_l
params.description: (bool) If `True`, perform the multiplication `P @ L`.

params.name: overwrite_a
params.description: (bool) Allow overwriting data in `a` (may enhance performance)

params.name: check_finite
params.description: (bool) Whether to check that the input matrices contain only finite numbers. Disabling may give a performance gain, but may result in problems (crashes, non-termination) if the inputs do contain infinities or NaNs.

cards.returns: tuple: `(P, L, U)` if `permute_l == False`, otherwise `(PL, U)`. `P` is a `cupy.ndarray` storing permutation matrix with dimension `(M, M)`. `L` is a `cupy.ndarray` storing lower triangular or trapezoidal matrix with unit diagonal with dimension `(M, K)` where `K = min(M, N)`. `U` is a `cupy.ndarray` storing upper triangular or trapezoidal matrix with dimension `(K, N)`. `PL` is a `cupy.ndarray` storing permuted `L` matrix with dimension `(M, K)`.

cards.summary: LU decomposition.
cards.description:
Decompose a given two-dimensional square matrix into `P * L * U`,
where `P` is a permutation matrix,  `L` lower-triangular with
unit diagonal elements, and `U` upper-triangular matrix.

params.name: a
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) The input matrix with dimension `(M, N)`

params.name: overwrite_a
params.description: (bool) Allow overwriting data in `a` (may enhance performance)

params.name: check_finite
params.description: (bool) Whether to check that the input matrices contain only finite numbers. Disabling may give a performance gain, but may result in problems (crashes, non-termination) if the inputs do contain infinities or NaNs.

cards.returns: tuple: `(lu, piv)` where `lu` is a `cupy.ndarray` storing `U` in its upper triangle, and `L` without unit diagonal elements in its lower triangle, and `piv` is a `cupy.ndarray` storing pivot indices representing permutation matrix `P`. For `0 <= i < min(M,N)`, row `i` of the matrix was interchanged with row `piv[i]`
pitfalls: Factor once with `lu_factor` and reuse the `(lu, piv)` tuple in `lu_solve` for many right-hand sides; this is cheaper than calling `solve` repeatedly.
`check_finite=True` by default, which scans the input for inf/nan and forces a device sync. Pass `check_finite=False` in hot loops.

cards.summary: Compressed Sparse Row matrix.
cards.description:
This can be instantiated in several ways.

`csr_matrix(D)`
    `D` is a rank-2 `cupy.ndarray`.
`csr_matrix(S)`
    `S` is another sparse matrix. It is equivalent to `S.tocsr()`.
`csr_matrix((M, N), [dtype])`
    It constructs an empty matrix whose shape is `(M, N)`. Default dtype
    is float64.
`csr_matrix((data, (row, col)))`
    All `data`, `row` and `col` are one-dimensional
    `cupy.ndarray`.
`csr_matrix((data, indices, indptr))`
    All `data`, `indices` and `indptr` are one-dimensional
    `cupy.ndarray`.
pitfalls: Only bool, float32, float64, complex64 and complex128 values are supported. Integer data raises `ValueError`; cast to float first.
Create it on the GPU from `(data, indices, indptr)` CuPy arrays, from a dense CuPy array, or from a SciPy sparse matrix (copied to the device).
`csr_matrix * x` is a matrix product (SciPy spmatrix semantics), but `csr_array * x` is elementwise. Use `A @ x` to be unambiguous.
Index arrays are int32 by default, and some cuSPARSE/cuSOLVER paths (e.g. `spsolve`) require int32 indices.

import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
import cupyx.scipy.sparse as sp

data = cp.asarray([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
indices = cp.asarray([0, 2, 1, 2], dtype=cp.int32)
indptr = cp.asarray([0, 2, 3, 4], dtype=cp.int32)
A = sp.csr_matrix((data, indices, indptr), shape=(3, 3))
x = cp.asarray([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
y = A @ x                                         # cuSPARSE SpMV
assert np.allclose(y.get(), [3.0, 3.0, 4.0])
assert np.allclose(A.toarray().get(), [[1, 0, 2], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 4]])

params.description: (ndarray) Starting vector for iteration. If `None`, a random unit vector is used.

params.description: (int) The number of Lanczos vectors generated. Must be `k + 1 < ncv < n`. If `None`, default value is used.

Needs `k < n`. For small dense problems, `cupy.linalg.eigh` is simpler and faster.

import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
import cupyx.scipy.sparse as sp
from cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh

n = 100
A = sp.diags([-1.0, 2.0, -1.0], [-1, 0, 1], shape=(n, n), format='csr')
w = eigsh(A, k=3, which='LA', return_eigenvectors=False)
expected = 2 - 2 * np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(n - 2, n + 1) / (n + 1))   # analytic spectrum
assert np.allclose(np.sort(w.get()), np.sort(expected), atol=1e-6)

    Systems on NVIDIA Tesla GPUs", ICCS 2009 (2009).

params.description: (int) Maximum number of iterations.

params.name: M
params.description: (ndarray, spmatrix or LinearOperator) Preconditioner for `A`. The preconditioner should approximate the inverse of `A`. `M` must be `cupy.ndarray`, `cupyx.scipy.sparse.spmatrix` or `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator`.

import numpy as np
import cupy as cp

cards.summary: Locally Optimal Block Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient Method (LOBPCG)
cards.description:
LOBPCG is a preconditioned eigensolver for large symmetric positive
definite (SPD) generalized eigenproblems.

params.name: A
params.description: (array-like) The symmetric linear operator of the problem, usually a sparse matrix. Can be of the following types - cupy.ndarray - cupyx.scipy.sparse.csr_matrix - cupy.scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator

params.name: X
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) Initial approximation to the `k` eigenvectors (non-sparse). If `A` has `shape=(n,n)` then `X` should have shape `shape=(n,k)`.

params.name: B
params.description: (array-like) The right hand side operator in a generalized eigenproblem. By default, `B = Identity`. Can be of following types: - cupy.ndarray - cupyx.scipy.sparse.csr_matrix - cupy.scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator

params.name: M
params.description: (array-like) Preconditioner to `A`; by default `M = Identity`. `M` should approximate the inverse of `A`. Can be of the following types: - cupy.ndarray - cupyx.scipy.sparse.csr_matrix - cupy.scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator

params.name: Y
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) `n-by-sizeY` matrix of constraints (non-sparse), `sizeY < n` The iterations will be performed in the B-orthogonal complement of the column-space of Y. Y must be full rank.

params.name: tol
params.description: (float) Solver tolerance (stopping criterion). The default is `tol=n*sqrt(eps)`.

params.name: maxiter
params.description: (int) Maximum number of iterations. The default is `maxiter = 20`.

params.name: largest
params.description: (bool) When True, solve for the largest eigenvalues, otherwise the smallest.

params.name: verbosityLevel
params.description: (int) Controls solver output. The default is `verbosityLevel=0`.

params.name: retLambdaHistory
params.description: (bool) Whether to return eigenvalue history. Default is False.

params.name: retResidualNormsHistory
params.description: (bool) Whether to return history of residual norms. Default is False.

cards.notes:

the return tuple has the following format

cards.signature: lsmr(A, b, x0=None, damp=0.0, atol=1e-06, btol=1e-06, conlim=100000000.0, maxiter=None)
cards.summary: Iterative solver for least-squares problems.
cards.description:
lsmr solves the system of linear equations `Ax = b`. If the system
is inconsistent, it solves the least-squares problem `min ||b - Ax||_2`.
A is a rectangular matrix of dimension m-by-n, where all cases are
allowed: m = n, m > n, or m < n. B is a vector of length m.
The matrix A may be dense or sparse (usually sparse).

params.name: A
params.description: (ndarray, spmatrix or LinearOperator) The real or complex matrix of the linear system. `A` must be `cupy.ndarray`, `cupyx.scipy.sparse.spmatrix` or `cupyx.scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator`.

params.name: b
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) Right hand side of the linear system with shape `(m,)` or `(m, 1)`.

params.name: x0
params.description: (cupy.ndarray) Starting guess for the solution. If None zeros are used.

params.name: damp
params.description: (float) Damping factor for regularized least-squares. `lsmr` solves the regularized least-squares problem :: min ||(b) - ( A )x|| ||(0) (damp*I) ||_2 where damp is a scalar. If damp is None or 0, the system is solved without regularization.

params.name: atol
params.description: (float) Stopping tolerances. `lsmr` continues iterations until a certain backward error estimate is smaller than some quantity depending on atol and btol.

params.name: btol
params.description: (float) Stopping tolerances. `lsmr` continues iterations until a certain backward error estimate is smaller than some quantity depending on atol and btol.

params.name: conlim
params.description: (float) `lsmr` terminates if an estimate of `cond(A)` i.e. condition number of matrix exceeds `conlim`. If `conlim` is None, the default value is 1e+8.

params.name: maxiter
params.description: (int) Maximum number of iterations.

cards.returns: tuple: - `x` (ndarray): Least-square solution returned. - `istop` (int): istop gives the reason for stopping:: 0 means x=0 is a solution. 1 means x is an approximate solution to A*x = B, according to atol and btol. 2 means x approximately solves the least-squares problem according to atol. 3 means COND(A) seems to be greater than CONLIM. 4 is the same as 1 with atol = btol = eps (machine precision) 5 is the same as 2 with atol = eps. 6 is the same as 3 with CONLIM = 1/eps. 7 means ITN reached maxiter before the other stopping conditions were satisfied. - `itn` (int): Number of iterations used. - `normr` (float): `norm(b-Ax)` - `normar` (float): `norm(A^T (b - Ax))` - `norma` (float): `norm(A)` - `conda` (float): Condition number of A. - `normx` (float): `norm(x)`

Find the solution to a large, sparse, linear system of equations.
The function solves `Ax = b`. Given two-dimensional matrix `A` is
decomposed into `Q * R`.

You can easily calculate the fourth element by `norm(b - Ax)` and the ninth element by `norm(x)`.

cards.description:
This object ensures the validity of resources during use and releases them when they are no longer needed to prevent misuse.

This object encompasses all functionalities of function-form APIs `fft`,
`ifft`, `rfft`, and `irfft`, which are convenience wrappers around it.
The stateful object also allows for the amortization of preparatory costs when the same
FFT operation is to be performed on multiple operands with the same problem
specification (see `reset_operand`, `reset_operand_unchecked`,
and `create_key` for more details).

Using the stateful object typically involves the following steps:

1. **Problem Specification**: Initialize the object with a defined operation and
   options.
2. **Preparation**: Use `plan` to determine the best algorithmic implementation
   for this specific FFT operation.
3. **Execution**: Perform the FFT computation with `execute`, which can be either
   forward or inverse FFT transformation.
4. **Resource Management**: Ensure all resources are released either by explicitly
   calling `free` or by managing the stateful object within a context manager.

Detailed information on each step described above can be obtained by passing in a
`logging.Logger` object to `FFTOptions` or by setting the appropriate
options in the root logger object, which is used by default:

import cupy as cp
import nvmath
import math

B, N = 256, 1024
a = cp.random.rand(B, N, dtype=cp.float64) + 1j * cp.random.rand(B, N, dtype=cp.float64)

cards.description:
This object ensures the validity of resources during use and releases them when they are no longer needed to prevent misuse.

This object encompasses all functionality of the function-form API
`nvmath.linalg.direct_solver`, which is a
convenience wrapper around it. The stateful object also allows amortization of preparatory
costs (for example `plan` and an LU `factorize`) when the same size and layout
are reused, including after `reset_operands` to update `a`/`b`.

Using the stateful object typically involves the following steps:

1. **Problem specification**: Initialize the object with `a`, `b`, and optional
   `options` / `execution` / `stream`.
2. **Preparation**: `plan` in preparation for factorization (see **Semantics**).
3. **Execution**: `factorize`, then `solve` to obtain `x` (or `solve`
   again with the same `a` and an updated `b` after `reset_operands` when the
   matrix or RHS values change without recreating the solver).
4. **Resource management**: Release resources with `free` or by using a `with` block.

More detail on what each phase is doing (planning, factorization, and solve) can be
seen in the logs by passing a `logging.Logger` in `DirectSolverOptions`,
or by configuring the root logger that `DirectSolverOptions` uses by default, for
>>> import logging
>>> logging.basicConfig(
...     level=logging.INFO,
...     format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(message)s",
...     datefmt="%m-%d %H:%M:%S",
... )

cards.notes:
The semantics of the matrix multiplication follows `numpy.matmul` semantics, with some restrictions on
    broadcasting. In addition, the semantics for the fused matrix addition are described below.


        For narrow-precision formats (FP8, MXFP8, NVFP4), some of the rules below are
        restricted — see the `narrow-precision` section for details.

    * For in-place matrix multiplication (where the result is written into `c`) the result has the same shape as `c`.
    * If arguments `a` and `b` are matrices, they are multiplied according to the rules of matrix multiplication.
    * If argument `a` is 1-D, it is promoted to a matrix by prefixing `1` to its dimensions. After matrix
      multiplication, the prefixed `1` is removed from the result's dimensions if the operation is not in-place.
    * If argument `b` is 1-D, it is promoted to a matrix by appending `1` to its dimensions. After matrix
      multiplication, the appended `1` is removed from the result's dimensions if the operation is not in-place.
    * If `a` or `b` is N-D (N > 2), then the operand is treated as a batch of matrices. If both `a` and `b` are N-D,
      their batch dimensions must match. If exactly one of `a` or `b` is N-D, the other operand is broadcast.
    * The operand for the matrix addition `c` may be a matrix of shape (M, 1) or (M, N), or the batched versions
      (..., M, 1) or (..., M, N). Here M and N are the dimensions of the result of the matrix multiplication. If N = 1, the
      columns of `c` are broadcast for the addition; the rows of `c` are never broadcast. If batch dimensions are not
      present, `c` is broadcast across batches as needed. If the operation is in-place, `c` cannot be broadcast since
      it must be large enough to hold the result.
    * Similarly, when operating on a batch, auxiliary outputs are 3-D for all epilogs. Therefore, epilogs that return 1-D
      vectors of length N in non-batched mode return 3-D matrices of size (batch, N, 1) in batched mode.

    For narrow-precision operations (FP8 and lower), further restrictions apply;
    see the narrow-precision support section below.

    Matrix multiplication with narrow-precision operands is supported, in FP8, MXFP8, and NVFP4 formats.

    **FP8 and MXFP8**

    FP8 and MXFP8 use `float8_e4m3fn` or `float8_e5m2` data types. The difference is the scaling mode:
    FP8 (`block_scaling=False`) uses per-tensor scaling where a single scalar scale is applied to each operand;
    MXFP8 (`block_scaling=True`) uses microscaling with 32-element blocks arranged in 128x128 tiles.


        FP8 and MXFP8 matrix multiplication requires **CUDA Toolkit 12.8 or newer**.
        **FP8 requires a device with compute capability 8.9 or higher** (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell or newer architecture).
        **MXFP8 requires a device with compute capability 10.0 or higher** (Blackwell or newer architecture).
        Please refer to the compute capability table (https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus)
        to check the compute capability of your device.

    For FP8 operations:

    * For each operand a scaling factor needs to be specified via `quantization_scales` argument.
    * Maximum absolute value of the result (amax) can be requested via
      `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.result_amax` option in `options` argument.
    * Custom result type (both FP8 and non-FP8) can be requested via
      `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.result_type` option in `options` argument.

    For MXFP8 operations:

    * 1-D (vector) operands are not supported. Both `a` and `b` must be at least 2-D matrices.
    * Broadcasting of batch dimensions is not supported. The batch shapes of `a` and `b` must match exactly.
    * All operand dimensions (M, N, K) must be multiples of 128.
    * `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.block_scaling` option must be set to `True` and
      block scaling factors need to be specified via `quantization_scales` argument.
      Utilities in `nvmath.linalg.advanced.helpers.matmul` can be used to create and modify
      block scaling factors, see e.g. `nvmath.linalg.advanced.helpers.matmul.create_mxfp8_scale`.
    * When the result type is a narrow-precision data type, the auxiliary output `"d_out_scale"`
      will be returned containing the scales used for result quantization.

    *Layout Requirements*

    Due to the requirements of narrow-precision GEMM kernels, the contracting dimension
    K must be contiguous (stride-1) for both operands. The following layout constraints
    apply to both FP8 and MXFP8:

    * Operand `a` must be `(..., M, K)` with `stride[-1] == 1` and
      `stride[-2] >= K` (row-major).  The leading dimension (`stride[-2]`) can be
      larger than `K` to support sliced or padded views.

    * Operand `b` must be `(..., K, N)` with `stride[-2] == 1` and
      `stride[-1] >= K` (column-major).  The leading dimension (`stride[-1]`) can
      be larger than `K` to support sliced or padded views.


        Epilog support for MXFP8 is still evolving in the underlying cuBLASLt library,
        so not every combination of epilog, data type, and layout is guaranteed to work.
        If running into unsupported combinations, a cuBLASLt error will be raised
        either at planning time or at execution time that will reveal the
        root cause. These gaps are expected to be filled in future cuBLASLt releases.

    For more details on the FP8 and MXFP8 formats in cuBLAS,
    see the cublasLtMatmul documentation (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/#cublasltmatmul).

    **NVFP4**

        NVFP4 support.

    NVFP4 uses `float4_e2m1fn_x2` data type with block scaling (16-element blocks arranged in 128x64 tiles).


        NVFP4 matrix multiplication currently requires **CUDA Toolkit 12.8 or newer**,
        **a device with compute capability 10.0 or higher** (Blackwell or newer architecture),
        and **PyTorch 2.9 or newer** for `float4_e2m1fn_x2` dtype support.
        Please refer to the compute capability table (https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus)
        to check the compute capability of your device.

    For NVFP4 operations:

    * 1-D (vector) operands are not supported. Both `a` and `b` must be at least 2-D matrices.
    * Broadcasting of batch dimensions is not supported. The batch shapes of `a` and `b` must match exactly.
    * The outer dimensions of `a` and `b` (M and N) must be multiples of 128,
      and the contracting dimension K must be a multiple of 64.
    * `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.block_scaling` option must be set to `True` and
      block scaling factors need to be specified via `quantization_scales` argument.
    * When the result type is a narrow-precision data type, the auxiliary output `"d_out_scale"`
      will be returned containing the scales used for result quantization.

    *Layout and Packing Requirements*

    FP4 data is per-byte packed: `float4_e2m1fn_x2` stores 2 FP4 values per byte.
    The block scaling (VEC16_UE4M3) assigns one scale factor per 16 consecutive elements
    along the innermost (stride-1) dimension of each operand. The layout requirements
    below ensure that this innermost dimension corresponds to the contracting dimension K
    for both operands.

    * Operand `a` must be `(..., M, K//2)` with `stride[-1] == 1` and
      `stride[-2] >= K//2`, i.e., row-wise packed along K. Note that the
      leading dimension (`stride[-2]`) can be larger than `K//2` to support
      sliced views, as long as the stride remains 16-byte aligned.

    * Operand `b` must be `(..., K//2, N)` with `stride[-2] == 1` and
      `stride[-1] >= K//2`, i.e., column-wise packed along K. Note that the
      leading dimension (`stride[-1]`) can be larger than `K//2` to support
      sliced views, as long as the stride remains 16-byte aligned.

    If your data has the stride-1 axis along a dimension other than K,
    you must repack it before calling `matmul`.

    When the result type is also FP4, the output is packed along a dimension that
    depends on the result layout order:

    * **Row-major result**: packed along N — shape `(..., M, N//2)`, strides `(..., N//2, 1)`.
    * **Column-major result**: packed along M — shape `(..., M//2, N)`, strides `(..., 1, M//2)`.

    The result layout order is determined by the following priority:

    1. If `c` is provided, the result inherits `c`'s layout order.
    2. Otherwise, if the epilog requests a specific layout, that layout is used.
    3. Otherwise, the result inherits `a`'s layout order as a fallback.

    *Epilog Support*

    NVFP4 matmul supports epilogs. The following have been verified:

    * `RELU`, `GELU` -- with both row-major and column-major output.
    * `BIAS`, `RELU_BIAS`, `GELU_BIAS` -- with column-major output only
      (`BIAS` with `float16` C/D requires cuBLASLt >= 13.0).

        so not every combination of epilog, data type, and layout is guaranteed to work.
        If running into unsupported combinations, a cuBLASLt error will be raised
        either at planning time or at execution time that will reveal the
        root cause. These gaps are expected to be filled in future cuBLASLt releases.

cards.description:
Scales can only be set for narrow-precision (FP8 and lower) matrices.

**FP8 operations** (`block_scaling=False`, per-tensor scaling):

* Scale format: **scalar** (integer or float) or single-element tensor
  of shape `()` or `(1,)`
* A single scale value is applied to the entire tensor.

**MXFP8 operations** (`block_scaling=True`, microscaling with FP8 operands):

* Scale format: **1D tensor** with layout matching cuBLAS MXFP8 requirements
* Scale dtype: `uint8` (interpreted as UE8M0 values by cuBLAS)
* A scale value `x` causes cuBLAS to multiply the respective
  block by `2^{x-127}`.

**NVFP4 operations** (`block_scaling=True`, block scaling with FP4 operands):

* Scale format: **1D tensor** with layout matching cuBLAS NVFP4 requirements
* Scale dtype: `float8_e4m3fn` (interpreted by cuBLAS as unsigned UE4M3 values,
  i.e. the bit sign is ignored).
* FP4 only supports block scaling; `block_scaling=False` is not supported for FP4.
cards.notes:
MXFP8 and NVFP4 use "block scaling" where each block of elements has its own
scale factor, as opposed to FP8 which uses a single per-tensor scale.
When `block_scaling=True`, tensor scales are required; scalar
scales are not allowed.

When scales are provided as tensors, they must be from the same package
and on the same memory space (CPU or GPU device) as the operands of the matmul.

cards.notes:
The semantics of the matrix multiplication follows `numpy.matmul` semantics, with some restrictions on
    broadcasting. In addition, the semantics for the fused matrix addition are described below.


        For narrow-precision formats (FP8, MXFP8, NVFP4), some of the rules below are
        restricted — see the `narrow-precision` section for details.

    * For in-place matrix multiplication (where the result is written into `c`) the result has the same shape as `c`.
    * If arguments `a` and `b` are matrices, they are multiplied according to the rules of matrix multiplication.
    * If argument `a` is 1-D, it is promoted to a matrix by prefixing `1` to its dimensions. After matrix
      multiplication, the prefixed `1` is removed from the result's dimensions if the operation is not in-place.
    * If argument `b` is 1-D, it is promoted to a matrix by appending `1` to its dimensions. After matrix
      multiplication, the appended `1` is removed from the result's dimensions if the operation is not in-place.
    * If `a` or `b` is N-D (N > 2), then the operand is treated as a batch of matrices. If both `a` and `b` are N-D,
      their batch dimensions must match. If exactly one of `a` or `b` is N-D, the other operand is broadcast.
    * The operand for the matrix addition `c` may be a matrix of shape (M, 1) or (M, N), or the batched versions
      (..., M, 1) or (..., M, N). Here M and N are the dimensions of the result of the matrix multiplication. If N = 1, the
      columns of `c` are broadcast for the addition; the rows of `c` are never broadcast. If batch dimensions are not
      present, `c` is broadcast across batches as needed. If the operation is in-place, `c` cannot be broadcast since
      it must be large enough to hold the result.
    * Similarly, when operating on a batch, auxiliary outputs are 3-D for all epilogs. Therefore, epilogs that return 1-D
      vectors of length N in non-batched mode return 3-D matrices of size (batch, N, 1) in batched mode.

    For narrow-precision operations (FP8 and lower), further restrictions apply;
    see the narrow-precision support section below.

    Matrix multiplication with narrow-precision operands is supported, in FP8, MXFP8, and NVFP4 formats.

    **FP8 and MXFP8**

    FP8 and MXFP8 use `float8_e4m3fn` or `float8_e5m2` data types. The difference is the scaling mode:
    FP8 (`block_scaling=False`) uses per-tensor scaling where a single scalar scale is applied to each operand;
    MXFP8 (`block_scaling=True`) uses microscaling with 32-element blocks arranged in 128x128 tiles.


        FP8 and MXFP8 matrix multiplication requires **CUDA Toolkit 12.8 or newer**.
        **FP8 requires a device with compute capability 8.9 or higher** (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell or newer architecture).
        **MXFP8 requires a device with compute capability 10.0 or higher** (Blackwell or newer architecture).
        Please refer to the compute capability table (https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus)
        to check the compute capability of your device.

    For FP8 operations:

    * For each operand a scaling factor needs to be specified via `quantization_scales` argument.
    * Maximum absolute value of the result (amax) can be requested via
      `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.result_amax` option in `options` argument.
    * Custom result type (both FP8 and non-FP8) can be requested via
      `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.result_type` option in `options` argument.

    For MXFP8 operations:

    * 1-D (vector) operands are not supported. Both `a` and `b` must be at least 2-D matrices.
    * Broadcasting of batch dimensions is not supported. The batch shapes of `a` and `b` must match exactly.
    * All operand dimensions (M, N, K) must be multiples of 128.
    * `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.block_scaling` option must be set to `True` and
      block scaling factors need to be specified via `quantization_scales` argument.
      Utilities in `nvmath.linalg.advanced.helpers.matmul` can be used to create and modify
      block scaling factors, see e.g. `nvmath.linalg.advanced.helpers.matmul.create_mxfp8_scale`.
    * When the result type is a narrow-precision data type, the auxiliary output `"d_out_scale"`
      will be returned containing the scales used for result quantization.

    *Layout Requirements*

    Due to the requirements of narrow-precision GEMM kernels, the contracting dimension
    K must be contiguous (stride-1) for both operands. The following layout constraints
    apply to both FP8 and MXFP8:

    * Operand `a` must be `(..., M, K)` with `stride[-1] == 1` and
      `stride[-2] >= K` (row-major).  The leading dimension (`stride[-2]`) can be
      larger than `K` to support sliced or padded views.

    * Operand `b` must be `(..., K, N)` with `stride[-2] == 1` and
      `stride[-1] >= K` (column-major).  The leading dimension (`stride[-1]`) can

        If running into unsupported combinations, a cuBLASLt error will be raised
        either at planning time or at execution time that will reveal the
        root cause. These gaps are expected to be filled in future cuBLASLt releases.

    For more details on the FP8 and MXFP8 formats in cuBLAS,
    see the cublasLtMatmul documentation (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/#cublasltmatmul).

    **NVFP4**

        NVFP4 support.

    NVFP4 uses `float4_e2m1fn_x2` data type with block scaling (16-element blocks arranged in 128x64 tiles).

    * 1-D (vector) operands are not supported. Both `a` and `b` must be at least 2-D matrices.
    * Broadcasting of batch dimensions is not supported. The batch shapes of `a` and `b` must match exactly.
    * The outer dimensions of `a` and `b` (M and N) must be multiples of 128,

    * `nvmath.linalg.advanced.MatmulOptions.block_scaling` option must be set to `True` and

The `\operatorname{op}_h` and `\operatorname{op}_t` operators optionally specify transpose/hermitian or transpose operations respectively via the `qualifiers` argument.

A stateful object can be used to amortize the cost of preparation (planning in the
case of matrix multiplication) across multiple executions (also see the

The function-form API `matmul` is a convenient alternative to using stateful
objects for *single* use (the user needs to perform just one matrix multiplication, for
example), in which case there is no possibility of amortizing preparatory costs. The
function-form APIs are just convenience wrappers around the stateful object APIs.

1. **Problem Specification**: Initialize the object with a defined operation and
   options.
2. **Preparation**: Use `plan` to determine the best algorithmic implementation

3. **Execution**: Perform the matrix multiplication computation with `execute`.
4. **Resource Management**: Ensure all resources are released either by explicitly
   calling `free` or by managing the stateful object within a context manager.

Detailed information on what's happening in the various phases described above can be
obtained by passing in a `logging.Logger` object to `MatmulOptions` or by
setting the appropriate options in the root logger object, which is used by default:

cards.notes:
The complex conjugate operation is mutually exclusive with prolog since it can be
absorbed into the prolog.

Currently only in-place sparse matrix multiplication is supported, so operand `c`
must be provided. This restriction will be removed in a future release.

    The semantics of the matrix multiplication follows `numpy.matmul` semantics, with some restrictions on
    broadcasting. In addition, the semantics for the fused matrix addition are described below.

    * For in-place matrix multiplication (where the result is written into `c`) the result has the same shape as `c`.
    * The operand `a` must be a sparse matrix or batched sparse matrix. Popular named formats like BSC, BSR, COO,
      CSR, ...  are supported in addition to custom formats defined using the UST DSL.
    * The operands `b` and `c` must be "dense" matrices (that is, their layout is strided).
    * If the operands `a` and `b` are matrices, they are multiplied according to the rules of matrix
      multiplication.
    * If argument `b` is 1-D, it is promoted to a matrix by appending `1` to its dimensions. After matrix
      multiplication, the appended `1` is removed from the result's dimensions if the operation is not in-place.
    * If `a` or `b` is N-D (N > 2), then the operand is treated as a batch of matrices. If both `a` and `b`
      are N-D, their batch dimensions must match. If exactly one of `a` or `b` is N-D, the other operand is
      broadcast.
    * The operand for the matrix addition `c` must be a matrix of shape (M, N), or the batched equivalent
      (..., M, N). Here M and N are the dimensions of the result of the matrix multiplication. If batch dimensions
      are not present, `c` is broadcast across batches as needed. If the operation is in-place, `c` cannot be
      broadcast since it must be large enough to hold the result.

cards.notes:
\

    (RHS) `b`.

    * In the simplest version with no batching, `a` is sparse (square) matrix of size `n` in Compressed Sparse Row (CSR)
      format, and `b` is a dense vector or matrix. A matrix (2D ndarray or tensor) in the RHS is treated as multiple
      column vectors corresponding to multiple solution vectors (i.e. `x` is the same shape as the RHS) to solve for.


    * Batching can be specified either **explicitly** or **implicitly**.

      * An **explicitly-batched** LHS is provided as a Python sequence of sparse CSR matrices `[a_0, a_1, ..., a_n]`.
        Likewise an explicitly-batched RHS is provided as a sequence of vectors or matrices `[b_0, b_1, ..., b_n]`.
        The solver will solve all `n` systems `a_i @ x_i = b_i` for the solution sequence `x_i`.
        Each sample in explicit batching can be of a different size, with the only constraint being that a given
        LHS size is consistent with that of its corresponding RHS.

      * An **implicitly-batched** LHS is provided as a higher-dimensional `N \geq 3D` sparse tensor in CSR format,
        where the leading `N - 2` dimensions are the batch dimensions, and the last two dimensions correspond to that
        of the `n \times n` sparse system. Currently, only PyTorch supports higher-dimensional sparse CSR tensors.
        Likewise, an implicitly-batched RHS is provided as a `N \geq 3D` dense ndarray/tensor, where the leading
        `N - 2` dimensions are the batch dimensions, and the last two dimensions correspond to the `n \times 1`
        vector or `n \times m` matrix for each sample. The solver solves `a_i @ x_i = b_i` for each sample
        `i` in the batch, and the solution `x` has the same shape as the RHS `b`.

      * Each sample `a_i` and `b_i` in the (explicitly- or implicitly-specified) batch are essentially
        treated as, and subject to, the same rules as the case with no batching.

      * The LHS and RHS batch specification is independent: for example, the LHS can be explicitly-batched while the
        RHS is implicitly-batched (or vice-versa). The same batch specification can be used for both as well.

      * The solution `x` always has the same form as the RHS `b`. It is a sequence of matrices or vectors if
        `b` is explicitly-batched, or a higher-dimensional ndarray/tensor if `b` is implicitly-batched.

import cupy as cp
import nvmath

M, N = 32, 64
a = cp.random.rand(M, M, N, N, dtype=cp.float32)
b = cp.random.rand(N, N, N, N, dtype=cp.float32)
c = cp.random.rand(M, M, N, N, dtype=cp.float32)

r = nvmath.tensor.binary_contraction(

o = nvmath.tensor.ContractionOptions(compute_type=compute_type)

    b = cp.random.rand(N, N, N, N)

b = np.random.rand(N, N, N, N)

r = nvmath.tensor.binary_contraction("ijkl,klmn->ijmn", a, b)
pitfalls: The expression comes first: `binary_contraction('ij,jk->ik', a, b)`. Optional `c`, `alpha` and `beta` compute `alpha * contraction + beta * c` in one call.
Operands stay in their package (CuPy in, CuPy out); for repeated contractions use the stateful `BinaryContraction`.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import cupy as cp
import nvmath

a = cp.random.rand(8, 16, 32, dtype=cp.float32)
b = cp.random.rand(32, 24, dtype=cp.float32)
c = nvmath.tensor.binary_contraction("bij,jk->bik", a, b)
assert c.shape == (8, 16, 24)
assert np.allclose(c.get(), np.einsum("bij,jk->bik", a.get(), b.get()), rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)

cards.signature: ternary_contraction(expr, a, b, c, *, d=None, alpha=1.0, beta=None, out=None, qualifiers=None, stream=None, options=None, execution=None)
cards.summary: Evaluate the Einstein summation convention for ternary contraction on the operands.
cards.description:
Explicit as well as implicit form is supported for the Einstein summation expression.

Additionally, the ternary contraction can be performed with
an additional operand, which is added to the result with a scale factor.

This function-form is a wrapper around the stateful
`TernaryContraction` object APIs and is meant for *single* use (the user needs
to perform just one ternary contraction, for example), in which case there is
no possibility of amortizing preparatory costs.

Detailed information on what's happening within this function can be obtained by passing
in a `logging.Logger` object to `ContractionOptions` or by setting the
appropriate options in the root logger object, which is used by default:

A user can select the desired logging level and, in general, take advantage of all of
the functionality offered by the Python `logging` module.

Further examples can be found in the nvmath/examples/tensor/contraction (https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvmath-python/tree/main/examples/tensor/contraction)
directory.

params.name: beta
